node_fields.description: A historian of Britain and its eighteenth-century empire. In her introduction to A New Imperial History, Wilson argues that imperial encounters helped constitute identities within Britain as well as overseas. Difference is an instrument of power, while identities are historically imposed and negotiated through legal status, gender, slavery and performance. She uses Chakrabarty’s challenge to Europe as history’s universal subject and Catherine Hall’s insistence on theorizing difference, without proposing that cultural analysis replace political or social history. Her account of colonial governmentality draws explicitly on Foucault. The later Strolling Players of Empire continues the inquiry through performance and colonial rule. Her work therefore connects cultural and political explanation; it does not treat every imperial setting as identical or empire as a one-way export from a metropolitan centre.

node_fields.description: A historian of Soviet social life and Stalinism. Fitzpatrick’s retrospective describes revisionism as a challenge to political-science domination and the totalitarian model, while retaining divisions among revisionists and between their generations. Her research follows mobility, everyday practices and people’s encounters with state power rather than treating society as a passive object of rule. In a comparative chapter coauthored with Alf Lüdtke, she takes Arendt’s atomization hypothesis as a question for empirical investigation: relationships could be broken and reconfigured, and participation also required attention to people’s emotional investments. The argument preserves Arendt’s recognition of support from below while questioning whether atomization adequately describes the societies concerned. Everyday Stalinism and the later political-team study connect social and political history; detailed everyday research alone does not establish a microhistory affiliation.

node_fields.description: A cultural historian of bodies, sexuality and death. Making Sex advances a historical account of the categories through which bodily difference was understood; the argument is controversial. Brooke Holmes challenges its division between premodern and modern bodies and, discussing Park, Nye, Cadden and King, argues that the evidence supports more varied and coexisting models. She also traces the book’s narrative of rupture to Foucault’s history of sexuality. That is a named scholarly interpretation of Laqueur, not a newly verified reading of all those originals. In his Berkeley interview, Laqueur explains another inquiry: the care and naming of the dead help construct enduring social relations. Making Sex, Solitary Sex and The Work of the Dead thus address historical meanings of embodied life while remaining distinct projects; the contested sex model is not adopted as a settled chronology.

node_fields.description: A historian of family, welfare and religion whose work asks how liberal authority was made through everyday institutions. In her 2009 intervention, Christie credits Ian McKay’s framework with connecting cultural and social research while disputing its periodization, statism and property-based account of individualism. She uses Bruce Curtis’s distinction between liberalism and governmentality to seek a more precise account of power. Churches, voluntary associations and households become sites of contested liberal values, including women’s participation as well as exclusion. Her appeal to Habermas’s civil society remains selective: she also points to work complicating the public/private division and insists on sentiment alongside rationalism. Engendering the State supplies one earlier research context; the religion books retain Michael Gauvreau’s coauthorship. The intervention revises the framework’s explanatory reach rather than simply replacing it with another single ideology.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern beliefs, social relations and changing attitudes toward nature. In his interview with Alan Macfarlane, Thomas explains how a historical puzzle about astrology led him toward anthropological comparison in Religion and the Decline of Magic. He recalls Christopher Hill and Tawney as important intellectual influences, and credits Lawrence Stone with encouraging the expansion of his review of Evans-Pritchard into the 1963 history-and-anthropology essay. His Annales interest centred on Febvre’s inquiry into people’s assumptions rather than hard quantitative history. He later characterized his own work as descriptive ethnography and acknowledged that his explanation of magic’s decline remained incomplete. Machielsen and Pfeffer’s reassessment supplies a separate critical reading of the 1971 book’s categories and continuing uses. These resources and disagreements locate a historical practice without making Thomas the founder of one unified anthropological school.

node_fields.description: A historian of gender, warfare, violence and emotion. Her work connects bodily experience with cultural meanings and unequal power. In her later methodological account of fear, Bourke asks what fear does: its expression follows learned conventions but can also change the feeling it articulates. She uses William Reddy’s emotives to avoid equating an emotional state with a mere report of it, while questioning a simple separation between mind and body. Narratives and bodily responses participate in social hierarchies, making historical context necessary to understanding emotion. Dismembering the Male and An Intimate History of Killing locate gender and embodied experience within war; these books’ complete arguments remain distinct from the primary methodological passages read. Her later cultural histories extend the question of how societies define and value persons rather than supplying timeless psychological laws.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian of religious practice, gender and embodiment. Bynum investigates fundamental cultural assumptions without reducing divergent medieval voices to one consistent worldview. Her retrospective credits Chenu and Grundmann with resources for studying religious thought and women’s agency; their works are not newly read here. Holy Feast and Holy Fast treats women’s religious writing as creative practice rather than merely male ventriloquism, while her body scholarship questions a simple equation of medieval Christianity with body-hating dualism. In “Why All the Fuss about the Body?” she engages sympathetically with Butler’s performative feminism but insists on comparing thinkers within their different historical settings. The point is neither that medieval theology already held modern gender theory nor that contemporary questions are irrelevant. Particularity, physical continuity and embodied personhood remain problems that discourse alone does not exhaust.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian whose emotional-communities approach treats feelings and their expression as socially valued practices in overlapping groups. “Worrying about Emotions in History” revisits Febvre’s call for an emotional history and challenges the grand narrative of progressive restraint associated with Elias. It also criticizes limits in Peter and Carol Stearns’s emotionology, especially the relation between prescriptive sources and emotional experience. Her proposal is not a claim that representations transparently reveal inner feelings. In the later interview she questions a rigid distinction between emotional regimes and refuges; Reddy’s own answer allowing plural regimes remains beside that objection. The entry therefore presents emotional communities as a methodological intervention in an ongoing debate, not a universal replacement for every other approach. Her medieval studies and selected books supply a bibliography distinct from the passages read.

node_fields.description: A Canadian archaeologist and ethnohistorian who sought to make Indigenous agency central to accounts of colonial encounters. Eric Wolf’s substantive reading of Natives and Newcomers identifies two connected projects: reconsidering the national narrative and bringing historical, archaeological and anthropological evidence into the same inquiry. Wolf also describes Trigger’s objection to an ethnographic present that removes social change from interpretation. This multidisciplinary programme does not remove the criticism of its categories. Emma LaRocque calls Trigger’s foreword to Sioui an example of containment and argues that the neo cross-cultural approach can distance and Other its subjects, while acknowledging its improvement on earlier racist scholarship. The Children of Aataentsic and Natives and Newcomers remain distinct milestones. Trigger is a settler scholar whose contribution and Indigenous criticism are presented together, without placing him in an Indigenous-authored field.

node_fields.description: A settler historian of Indigenous–newcomer relations, residential schooling and treaties. Shingwauk’s Vision combines institutional research and interviews, but Celia Haig-Brown’s review challenges the homogenization of experiences, the balance of explanatory sympathy and the handling of resistance. Those objections qualify the national synthesis rather than disappearing behind its breadth. Claude Gélinas reads Compact, Contract, Covenant as a history of political relationships through changing treaty-making, with Indigenous purposes and perspectives included rather than treaties treated solely as instruments of dispossession. He does not claim the book creates an entirely new general interpretation; his comparison with Arthur Ray concerns the contribution of a particular synthesis, not proof of intellectual influence. These named readings distinguish Miller’s institutional and political projects while keeping community testimony and knowledge outside the entry.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern Spain, political power and imperial comparison. Elliott’s comparative approach sought to unsettle national exceptionalisms without dissolving political choices into impersonal structures. Kagan and Parker’s scholarly memoir describes his attraction to Febvre’s integration of a region’s history and his qualified admiration for Braudel: he valued the wider vision while doubting its integration of structural analysis with events. Political biography remained important to his Olivares project. His criticism of microhistory’s representativeness was contested in turn. Ginzburg rejected a simple opposition of microhistory to macrohistory, while Natalie Zemon Davis defended the coexistence of Martin Guerre and Martin Luther within historical inquiry. These disagreements accompany the Atlantic and composite-monarchy studies rather than making Elliott an unqualified spokesman for either large-scale synthesis or political history alone.

node_fields.description: A social and cultural historian of religion, secularisation and unbelief. Brown’s work moved from class-based measurements of church participation toward the gendered and discursive conditions of Christian identity, with a sharp rupture proposed for the 1960s. That account remains contested. Jeremy Morris accepts criticism of inevitable modernization-to-decline stories while arguing that Brown and others narrow religion too far: institutional decline can coexist with persistent religious identity. Brown’s later “The Necessity of Atheism” approaches the problem from another direction. Using Charles Taylor as a critical foil, he argues that measuring secularity only through religious categories marginalizes lives lived without a god and that medieval disbelief should not be ruled out in advance. The intervention challenges both the assumed religious past and the categories used to describe the secular present; it does not establish a single universal measure of unbelief.

node_fields.description: A historian of the Dutch Republic, European Jews and the Enlightenment whose radical-Enlightenment interpretation gives philosophical ideas a strong explanatory role. Israel’s interview argues that Spinoza’s reception helped create a radical current committed to equality and criticism of religious authority, opposed to a moderate Enlightenment. David Bell credits Israel’s range and insistence on ideas while challenging inferences from similar ideas to transmission, from polemical labels to actual belief, and from radical proposals to revolutionary causation. Bell invokes contextual intellectual history as a methodological contrast, not proof that Skinner personally answered Israel. These disagreements qualify the thesis’s explanatory priority; neither the historian’s confidence nor his critics’ objections are turned into disciplinary consensus.

node_fields.description: A historian of modern Europe and the political organization of space. Maier treats territoriality as a historical resource: borders, sovereignty, technologies and institutions shape both decision-making and belonging. His interview explains why railways, telegraphs and other technologies matter without assuming that a networked world has abolished states. A conference report records Breuilly’s challenge to the coherence of an earlier “age of territoriality,” and Chatterjee’s account of colonial India’s overlapping sovereignties complicates any universal sequence. Maier’s own later account acknowledges more resistance to disappearing borders than he originally expected. His other research follows collective memory, trials and reparation after political violence. These are related inquiries into institutions and historical explanation, not a single prediction that globalization must dissolve political territory.

node_fields.description: A historian of gender, sexuality and urban life who joins cultural interpretation to material and social conditions. In her Minerva interview, Walkowitz recalls Hayden White’s supervision and his introduction of Foucault as resources for her research. She also identifies E. P. node_fields.description: A historian of international power who connects economic resources with military commitments and the changing position of states. node_fields.description: A historian of Scottish society, economy and diaspora whose slavery research places national history within Atlantic relationships. In “Did Slavery Make Scotia Great?” Devine returns to the controversy opened by Eric Williams while distinguishing profits from direct slave trading from the wider effects of plantation economies. Morton and Griffiths nonetheless question the nation as the automatic container of historical synthesis, explicitly discussing The Scottish Nation. These perspectives retain both the national synthesis and the question of how its frame relates to movement, empire and social differentiation.

node_fields.description: A historian of modern Germany who also examines the practice and public responsibilities of historical inquiry. In Defence of History defends evidence while refusing to make the profession immune to outside criticism. Its introduction accepts White’s objection to historians claiming sole authority to explain their own work and distinguishes this from accepting every postmodernist argument. His accounts of disease and German society connect institutions with inequality; his public source-criticism work in the Irving trial is a distinct intervention. These projects supply a historically situated defence of inquiry, not a neutral census of all narrative theory or proof that historians can recover the past without interpretive choices.

node_fields.description: A historian of Scottish society and environments whose work joins changing material constraints to changing perceptions of nature. In “Land and Sea,” Smout explicitly uses Wrigley’s account of energy capture and the transition from organic to fossil-fuel economies. The chapter also identifies Cronon’s city-and-hinterland history as a model for work still needed on Scottish cities. These are particular resources, not an assertion that every Scottish development follows an English or American pattern. His earlier green-consciousness lecture questions a simple story in which appreciation of Highland landscapes was imported into a previously indifferent society. The social syntheses remain important to the entry, but their national frame is also questioned in Morton and Griffiths’s historiographical discussion. node_fields.description: A historian of South Asia whose research connects colonial power with medicine, science and environment. This qualified use of theory accompanies his participation in the founding Subaltern Studies collective; neither connection licenses reading every later project as the application of a single school.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian of social relations, objects and the production of a remembered past. The opening of “Sacred Commodities” asks what makes relics exchangeable within a particular medieval setting, rather than assuming a timeless market for all objects. node_fields.description: A historian of cities, capitalism and environmental disaster. node_fields.description: A historian of European intellectual and cultural life who used psychoanalysis while resisting reduction of historical events to inner experience. In his 1997 interview, Gay describes Freud as an indispensable resource for studying interaction between psychological processes and external circumstances. These positions support a particular historian’s psychoanalytic practice, rather than a claim that psychoanalysis supplies a complete explanation of history.

node_fields.description: A social and oral historian concerned with how interviews change both historical evidence and research practice. node_fields.description: A historian of medicine and science who connects disease categories, institutions and changing social relations. node_fields.description: A medieval historian of conquest, institutions and historical categories. His 2001 article treats both race and ethnicity as social constructions and warns against using present administrative labels as ready-made historical explanations. It then compares medieval terminology and argues for the importance of culture, law, language and religion in making identities. Bartlett’s point is not simply that medieval writers lacked descent thinking: he examines genealogical idioms while emphasizing changeable identifications. His discussion of nationhood also separates collective identity from an automatic demand for sovereign statehood. Geraldine Heng later questions the sharpness of his distinction between medieval cultural difference and biological racism. That criticism remains alongside his argument, rather than turning either position into a consensus. The Making of Europe, Trial by Fire and Water and England under the Norman and Angevin Kings locate a wider programme whose complete monographs remain unread here.

node_fields.description: A literary theorist associated with New Historicism who studies literary form within historical relations. His retrospective account credits Raymond Williams with helping him connect Marxist literary criticism to the world in which works are made. He also values the formalist skills acquired in his earlier training, even as he challenged its exclusion of historical circumstances. In “Culture,” constraint and mobility depend on one another: improvisation and exchange help constitute cultural boundaries. This is more specific than treating context as a static background. His historical narratives also invite criticism. John Monfasani challenges The Swerve’s opposition between medieval darkness and Renaissance modernity and the evidence for Lucretius’s transformative influence; Greenblatt’s response explicitly defends the importance of the Renaissance and atomism. That dispute, alongside Maza’s disciplinary questions, qualifies the relationship between his literary practice and historians’ cultural history.
